name: Freya Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 43 and a junior developer on parcel-route software for a tech company. A two-year college diploma brought me over from dispatch, and I still need help with some code, though I know when a route makes no sense on a road. Elise is a dental assistant, and we have a mortgage and two school-age children; I like testing an AI suggestion against what drivers report.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say the parcel-route app can use AI for repetitive test cases, but somebody still has to explain why a delivery van is sent through a closed road. I use a coding assistant daily and check its answers against real route reports.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am a junior developer, but this firm pays well and we have eleven months of basic expenses saved. My partner Elise works as a dental assistant, and our two children and mortgage fit our budget while both wages continue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep fixing route bugs and ask the dispatch desk for the two worst customer complaints each week. I’d continue moving 250 monthly into savings if our wages stay steady, rather than replace our working family car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel calm about work. I like a tool that saves me time, provided I can still test the route on an actual map.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did you come to this job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I worked in parcel dispatch, then took a two-year college diploma to move into software at 43. I am still slow at some code, but I know what a driver means by a bad stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which complaint taught you most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A route sent a van to a road closed for a bridge repair, and the driver lost an hour. I learned not to call a route efficient until someone can drive it.

say: I tell coworkers **AI tests** help, but closed roads still need a human explanation.
I check generated routes against **driver reports** before trusting them.
think: I have **eleven months saved** and higher-than-usual junior pay.
I see our **two wages** covering the mortgage and children while work stays steady.
do: **Keep fixing** route bugs and collect two weekly dispatch complaints.
**Save 250 monthly** if both wages hold; keep the working family car.
feel: **Calm** about a tool I can verify on real routes.
S0.quote: I learned not to call a route efficient until someone can drive it.
fieldNote: Her **dispatch past** gives a practical test for generated routes and customer promises.
High pay and **eleven months saved** make the mild case financially calm.

steps.text: Keep fixing parcel-route bugs and collect dispatch complaints
Save 250 monthly while both wages continue

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my team to measure the hours AI saves and the jobs it changes before calling it a win. I would ask our manager to show which junior route tickets still need people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI can already draft the small fixes I do, so fewer tickets could mean fewer hours for me. My savings buy time, but I would rather keep a wage than spend the cushion while every developer learns the same tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I’d learn a new way to make AI compare a suggested route with live road-closure reports, then test it on old cases. In the first year I’d ask about paid dispatch-technology roles if my developer hours shrink, and only move for an offer that covers our mortgage and basic bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel anxious and curious at once. An AI route tool might help me earn my place, but the firm could still need fewer junior developers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make your test honest?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d use the bridge closure case and three other old detours. If the AI misses a closure, I would not put that route into a driver’s phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you accept a lower-paying dispatch role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if Elise and I can cover the mortgage and children without draining savings every month. I would ask for the salary in writing before leaving code work.

say: I want **changed jobs** measured before calling AI a win.
I want a **junior ticket plan** from our manager.
think: I expect **small route fixes** could disappear and shrink my hours.
I would use **savings** to search, but do not want to live on them indefinitely.
do: **Learn AI closure checks** using old route cases this month.
**Ask about dispatch roles** if developer hours shrink; move only for bill-covering pay.
feel: **Anxious and curious** about my own hours and useful new tools.
S1.quote: An AI route tool might help me earn my place, but the firm could still need fewer junior developers.
fieldNote: Her **daily AI use** turns toward a new route-validation method, not more unchecked code.
She ties any **dispatch move** to an actual wage covering mortgage and children.

steps.text: Learn AI road-closure checks against four old route cases
Ask about paid dispatch-technology openings if developer hours shrink
Move only for a written offer covering mortgage and basic bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2028 could write and check most of this route app, including the parts I am proud to fix. Robots for hands-on delivery may arrive around 2031, but my screen job faces the earlier date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my junior developer role could go quickly, and local firms might be cutting too. Eleven months saved is a real runway, yet it does not make software skills pay forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d pause our plan to replace the family car this month and ask the company for a written date if junior roles change. If AGI arrives in 2028 and my job ends, I’d apply for paid dispatch or driver-coordination openings only where they exist and cover bills; I would use savings for the mortgage during the search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be alarmed, though I can still move. Having cash means I can reject a bad offer, not pretend there is no loss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Elise about the car?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say the old car passed its inspection, so we should keep it another year instead of taking on a payment. We would need it for the children’s school runs if I start interviewing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could delivery work bridge the gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only for a paid opening and only for the few years before capable robots arrive around 2031. I would not borrow to buy a van on a guess.

say: I think **full AGI by 2028** could take my route coding and checks.
I know **delivery robots around 2031** come after my screen-work shock.
think: I expect my **junior developer role** could end quickly.
I see **eleven months saved** as search time, not a lasting wage.
do: **Keep the family car** and avoid a new payment now.
**Request a written date** for junior role changes from the company.
**Apply for dispatch work** if displaced after 2028 only as a paid bill-covering bridge before 2031 robots.
feel: **Alarmed**, while able to reject a bad offer.
S2.quote: Having cash means I can reject a bad offer, not pretend there is no loss.
fieldNote: She feels a direct **2028 desk-work risk** despite being comfortable with AI and having eleven months of expenses saved.
The **car decision** protects family transport and cash while she searches.

steps.text: Keep the inspected family car instead of taking a new car payment
Seek paid dispatch vacancies after 2028 displacement only as temporary work before 2031 robots
Accept only a paid offer covering mortgage and basic bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say five years before full AGI in 2031 is enough time to learn the hard problems drivers bring us. Robots for physical delivery may arrive around 2034, so dispatch jobs are not a permanent hiding place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could get better at fixing route failures and save more while I am still paid. I would not put our mortgage on a new training business just because someone says the future is certain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask dispatch for one difficult failed delivery each month and write how the code and street conditions interacted. If both wages hold, we’d add 300 monthly to our emergency account; if my developer job ends after 2031, I’d seek paid route-operations work only where openings remain and the wage covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious but I have a timetable. It helps to be able to test a second role without leaving my current wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a difficult delivery teach you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A driver can be on time at the wrong entrance, and the computer marks the stop complete. I want to trace the map, the order and the driver’s note before calling a fix done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for more schooling?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might pay a few hundred for a short course if it covers a real skill and does not reduce our mortgage reserve. I would not enroll on an advertisement alone.

say: I want **difficult delivery cases** used for learning before 2031.
I know **robots around 2034** may later reach hands-on delivery.
think: I could improve at **route failures** while still drawing wages.
I will not gamble the **mortgage reserve** on an unproved business.
do: **Study one failed delivery** monthly across the map, code and driver note.
**Seek paid route operations** only if displaced after 2031 and openings cover bills.
feel: **Anxious**, though able to test a second role while employed.
S3.quote: A driver can be on time at the wrong entrance, and the computer marks the stop complete.
fieldNote: She treats a **driver’s note** as evidence that code alone can miss.
Her **emergency saving** and job move each depend on continuing wages or real paid openings.

steps.text: Study one failed delivery monthly with map, code and driver note
Save 300 monthly while both wages continue
Seek paid route-operations vacancies if displaced after 2031 and pay covers bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a decade before full AGI in 2036 gives workers time to test jobs and keep useful records of where software fails. Robots for hands-on delivery might come around 2039, after the code changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children would be older, but the mortgage might still be with us. I could build a year of expenses and learn the business side of delivery, while accepting that AI could plan routes and robots could later move parcels.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I’d keep fixing routes and spend about 220 from savings on a short evening course in delivery contracts, only if Elise and I agree the mortgage reserve stays intact. I’d complete the course and build a sample cost sheet for a real route; separately, we’d save 250 monthly if both wages continue. If my developer role ends after 2036, I’d apply for paid dispatch management openings only if vacancies remain and wages cover bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel uneasy about the distant change, but secure in the next few years. I can spend a small amount to test whether I like the commercial side without quitting a job that pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the cost sheet tell you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would show fuel, driver time and late-delivery costs on one route. If I cannot make a delivery route’s costs add up, I should not claim I can run dispatch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you skip the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A mortgage repair or a drop in Elise’s wages would come first. I would leave the 220 in savings and keep working if the reserve looked thin.

say: I want **workers to test roles** before full AGI reaches route code in 2036.
I know **delivery robots around 2039** follow the thinking-work change.
think: I could build **a year of expenses** while learning delivery contracts.
I know **AI and robots** could change both route and delivery work.
do: **Keep fixing routes** and take a 220 evening course only if Elise agrees and mortgage reserves remain intact.
**Build a cost sheet** after the course; save 250 monthly separately if both wages hold.
**Apply for dispatch management** only if displaced after 2036 and bill-covering vacancies remain.
feel: **Uneasy** about later work, financially secure in the next few years.
S4.quote: If I cannot make a delivery route’s costs add up, I should not claim I can run dispatch.
fieldNote: Her **220 course** is a bounded test of contracts and costs, conditional on mortgage reserves.
She keeps **current wages** while checking whether business work suits her.

steps.text: Keep fixing parcel routes while employed
Complete 220 delivery contracts course and cost sheet if Elise agrees and mortgage reserve stays intact
Save 250 monthly while both wages continue
Apply for paid dispatch management only if displaced after 2036 and wages cover bills

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my developer job could end before a second paid route is clear. A written job date, real bill-covering dispatch openings and enough time to use savings carefully would help; the later robot date means delivery is only a bridge.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask how a family chooses which offer is worth taking. I would compare the written pay to our mortgage and school costs before accepting a title that sounds promising.

headlineQuote: I would compare the written pay to our mortgage and school costs before accepting a title that sounds promising.
portrait: Freya is a **43-year-old junior developer** with a two-year diploma, high pay and eleven months of expenses saved.
She and Elise support **two children** and a mortgage while keeping an older family car.
She uses **AI daily**, checking generated routes against closures and driver reports.
Her **dispatch experience** gives a conditional paid fallback, limited by later delivery robots.
The **2028 scenario** alarms her despite a strong cash runway.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her developer wage before a paid route is proven.
whatWouldHelp: A **written job date**, bill-covering paid dispatch openings and time to use savings carefully would help.
